abstract: The opioid epidemic continues to impose substantial public health burdens. Critical gaps remain in understanding how sex and individual differences contribute to opioid addiction-like behavior. Although previous clinical and preclinical work has identified sex and other individual differences in opioid-related outcomes, it remains unclear whether the magnitude of sex differences varies across behavioral domains and levels of individual addiction-like vulnerability. To address this gap, we analyzed data from 810 genetically diverse heterogeneous stock (HS) rats that underwent oxycodone self-administration under short-access (2h/day) and extended-access (12h/day) conditions. Addiction-like behavior was characterized across four domains comprising escalation of oxycodone intake, motivation to obtain oxycodone, tolerance to oxycodone-induced analgesia, and withdrawal-induced hyperalgesia. These measures were integrated into a composite Addiction Index (AI) to characterize individual addiction-like severity, with animals classified into four groups: resilient, mild, moderate, and severe. Sex differences were then examined across behavioral outcomes, AI groups, and experimental cohorts. Estrous-phase effects on motivation, relationships among behavioral dimensions, and within-session patterns of oxycodone intake were also examined. Females exhibited greater oxycodone intake and motivation than males following extended access, whereas pain-related behavioral outcomes showed greater associations across levels of addiction-like severity than between sexes. Although sex differences were observed for specific behavioral outcomes, further analyses provided no evidence that their magnitude varied across AI groups. Estrous phase did not significantly affect motivation for oxycodone. Pooled sex effects supported greater self-administration and motivation in females, whereas pooled sex effects for pain-related outcomes were not significant and showed varying degrees of between-cohort heterogeneity. Temporal features of oxycodone intake also differed by sex and were associated with addiction-like severity, with titration-phase intake showing the strongest association with the AI. Relationships among addiction-related behavioral dimensions were largely similar between females and males, although specific associations differed by sex and across AI groups. These findings demonstrate that sex and individual variability contribute in different ways to oxycodone addiction-like behavior. Female-biased differences were most apparent following extended access, whereas pain-related behavioral outcomes showed greater associations across levels of addiction-like severity. Together, these results highlight the importance of multidimensional phenotyping for characterizing sex and individual variability in opioid addiction-like behavior. Keywords: sex differences; individual differences, Heterogeneous Stock rats; estrous cycle; oxycodone; opioids; addiction-like behavior
